stem.en: In early Indian kingdoms, three matters come up: a case to be judged in a district, a law-and-order problem in a city, and the affairs of one village. Who dealt with each?

text.en: All three went to the king, because supreme authority rested with him.
All three went to the amātyas of the āḥāra, who had no other officers below them.
The district governor judged the case, the city governor kept order, and the grāmika led the village.
The grāmika judged the case, the district governor kept order in the city, and the king led the village.

explanation.en: District governors, or pradeśhikas, had judicial and administrative work. Cities had their own governors for revenue and law and order. Each village was led by a headman, the grāmika. Supreme authority rested with the king, but officers at provincial and local levels carried out the general administration.

hints.en: Each of the three matters goes to a different person.
Supreme authority is not the same as doing every job in person.
